profiles.meeting_scenario: AP-HP has invited a methodological advisor from CNEDiMTS to a brainstorming meeting about a possible coordination pilot for innovative medical device assessments after an internal review showed that local CODIMS evaluations often precede national recommendations by about a year while still reaching broadly similar conclusions. The context is a non-decision meeting: they are not approving a protocol yet, but generating practical ideas for how national and hospital-level assessment could exchange information earlier without duplicating work. The agenda is to brainstorm what a 'coordination pilot' should look like, which past device cases could be used to test it, what kind of shared materials would circulate, and how to describe alignment between local and national opinions. The expected outcome is a short list of candidate pilot concepts and a rough shared narrative for presenting the idea to their respective committees.

members.name: Dr. Claire Moreau
members.role: Deputy Head of Hospital Health Technology Assessment, AP-HP / CODIMS liaison
members.expertise: Hospital-based assessment of innovative medical devices, formulary entry workflows, early adoption governance
members.background: Claire is a pharmacist by training and has spent eight years coordinating evidence reviews for devices proposed for introduction across AP-HP hospitals, especially when clinicians want access before national reimbursement decisions are finalized.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to validate the usefulness of hospital-level assessment and protect AP-HP's ability to review devices early for operational planning, while avoiding any framing that makes CODIMS look like it acts prematurely or inconsistently.
hidden_assumptions: An 'early evaluation' is meaningful only relative to when a device could start being used or procured inside AP-HP, not relative to the publication date of a national opinion.
When comparing local and national recommendations, a device platform with minor commercial variants or adjacent use-cases is still practically the 'same device' for coordination purposes.
If two committees both end up broadly favorable or both broadly unfavorable, their opinions are 'consistent' even when restrictions on indication or implementation differ.
The useful coordination window starts as soon as a manufacturer or clinician approaches AP-HP with a concrete request, because that is when hospitals must begin internal assessment work.
A shared dossier should include pragmatic local material such as expected care pathway impact and early user feedback, even if it is not in the formal national template.

members.name: Dr. Julien Lefevre
members.expertise: National medical device appraisal methods, reimbursement file review, evidentiary standards for committee recommendations
members.background: Julien is a public health physician who supports national device assessments and regularly helps structure manufacturer submissions for committee review, with a focus on comparability across dossiers and clean methodological boundaries.
members.private_state: He wants any coordination pilot to be methodologically tidy and politically safe, showing that early exchange can improve preparedness without blurring the distinction between local operational decisions and national reimbursement appraisal.
hidden_assumptions: An 'early evaluation' is defined relative to the formal national appraisal timeline, especially the period before CNEDiMTS issues its recommendation.
A comparison between committees only makes sense when the exact device version and indication under review are matched, not just the same commercial family.
Two opinions are only truly 'consistent' if their access conditions, intended population, and evidence caveats materially align, not merely their overall favorability.
The relevant pre-national coordination window begins once a manufacturer has an identifiable national dossier or at least a formally recognizable intended claim.
A shared dossier should be a structured evidence synopsis compatible with national review conventions, excluding local procurement detail and anecdotal site experience unless explicitly formalized.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about creating a process for 'early evaluation' of innovative devices.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means assessment early enough to inform AP-HP purchasing, pilot use, and clinical adoption before hospital rollout.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means assessment occurring before CNEDiMTS publishes its recommendation within the national appraisal pathway.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds shared and high-level, and in this domain both meanings plausibly point to 'before the national opinion,' so neither participant feels a need to operationalize the reference point during an initial brainstorming meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: What qualifies as the 'same device' across committees
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss comparing opinions on 'the same device' and selecting candidate cases from prior assessments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes the same device platform across close model variants or hospital-relevant indication extensions if clinicians perceive them as one technology family.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 restricts comparison to the exact model-reference and claimed indication reviewed in the national file.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ordinary discussion, people routinely collapse device families into one label, especially when brainstorming examples; because both know the product names, the false sense of shared reference survives without explicit delimitation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the pilot should focus on cases where local and national opinions were 'consistent.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 counts opinions as consistent when they point in the same overall direction, such as both allowing use with some caveats or both expressing skepticism.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 counts opinions as consistent only when the recommended population, implementation conditions, and strength of reservations are substantively aligned.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Since the seed study already reports high consistency, the term arrives pre-legitimated; both participants assume they are preserving the existing conclusion rather than redefining a comparison rule.

misalignment_points.topic: Where the pre-national coordination window begins
misalignment_points.surface_form: They propose using the 'pre-CNEDiMTS window' to exchange information before the national opinion.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this window starts when AP-HP receives a concrete local request from clinicians or a manufacturer approaches the hospital for introduction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this window starts only once a manufacturer has initiated or clearly prepared a national reimbursement dossier with a defined claim.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are speaking about the period 'before CNEDiMTS,' and each treats their own starting point as institutionally obvious; because no one is assigning dates in the meeting, the timeline mismatch remains invisible.

turns.inner_thought: I need to position this as a sensible extension of what AP-HP already does well: we start assessment work as soon as there is a concrete request for introduction, because operational planning cannot wait. The point of early evaluation, for me, is to support local adoption and procurement choices in that period before national conclusions arrive, without suggesting CODIMS is jumping the gun. If I anchor this around the year we often have before CNEDiMTS opinions, it will sound collaborative rather than defensive.
turns.utterance: Thank you for coming, Julien. What I hoped we could do today is really just brainstorm. From our side, there seems to be a genuine opportunity to build a coordination pilot that preserves the value of hospital-level early evaluation, while making better use of the year we often have before CNEDiMTS opinions arrive. If we can describe that in a practical way, I think it could be useful for both sides.

turns.inner_thought: That framing is acceptable as long as we keep a clean line between local preparation and national appraisal. For me, early evaluation only really matters in relation to the national timeline, and the pre-CNEDiMTS window is the phase before the committee recommendation when an identifiable dossier or intended claim exists. I should emphasize exchange and preparedness, not any suggestion that local committees and CNEDiMTS are reviewing the same thing at the same stage.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think there is something worth exploring there. From the national side, the opportunity would be to improve exchange during the pre-CNEDiMTS window, so that reviewers are not discovering key issues too late in the appraisal process. If the pilot is framed around preparedness and better circulation of information, that feels constructive.

turns.inner_thought: We should start with examples that are easy to tell: technologies where CODIMS looked at the platform early, CNEDiMTS later reviewed what is practically the same device, and both landed in the same overall direction. I do not need to bog this down in tiny distinctions between variants or nuanced restrictions; for a proof of concept, broad alignment is enough and much easier to defend publicly.
turns.utterance: To make it manageable, I would start with three or four past cases where both committees looked at the same device and ended up broadly aligned. Those would be the easiest cases to present as a proof of concept, because we could show that earlier coordination might have saved time without changing the overall picture.

turns.inner_thought: That works if we are disciplined about case selection. I need cases where there was a clear national file, with a defined object of review, so we can reconstruct what was knowable before the recommendation. If she says the same device, I assume she means an exact match; otherwise the comparison becomes methodologically weak. Better to mention recent dossiers and available documentation.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. I would probably favor recent dossiers where the same device had a clear national file, because then we can more credibly reconstruct what information was available before the recommendation and what might realistically have been exchanged earlier.

turns.inner_thought: Valve platforms and navigation systems are ideal precisely because local demand appears before every model detail or use-case is stabilized in the national pathway. CODIMS often has to engage with the technology family as hospitals see it, not wait for each commercial or indication boundary to settle. I can hint at that without spelling it out.
turns.utterance: A few of the valve and navigation-system platforms come to mind as especially useful examples. In our experience, CODIMS often sees the main technology early, before everything is fully stabilized nationally, so they may give us a realistic picture of how a coordination pilot would actually work.

turns.inner_thought: Those families could work, but only if we can isolate instances where the same device was under review in a recognizable form and where the opinions were really consistent in their conditions, target population, and caveats. I do not want a pilot built on loose family resemblance or superficial agreement. Still, at this stage I can keep it broad.
turns.utterance: Yes, those families could be good examples, provided we choose instances where the opinions were really consistent and the intended claim was already recognizable by the time of exchange. If we can identify a few such cases, the pilot narrative will be much stronger.

turns.inner_thought: The shared material has to reflect real hospital needs, not just a stripped-down evidence table. When AP-HP starts assessment work, we need care pathway implications, implementation issues, and feedback from the first sites asking to use the device. That practical content is exactly what makes local early evaluation useful. I should pitch it as a light dossier so it sounds proportionate and not like we are inventing a parallel process.
turns.utterance: In terms of format, I wonder whether the pilot could revolve around a light dossier prepared during early evaluation. Nothing too heavy: an evidence summary, certainly, but also expected pathway impact and practical feedback from the first requesting sites. That would make the exchange concrete without creating a second full assessment process.

turns.inner_thought: A light dossier is acceptable if it remains structured and compatible with national review conventions. I need something standardized enough to map onto the pre-recommendation stage, not a bundle of procurement considerations or anecdotal impressions that could blur appraisal boundaries. I should encourage the format while quietly signaling the need for methodological discipline.
turns.utterance: I think a light dossier could be very helpful, yes, as long as it is standardized enough to plug into national review and can be linked to the stage before the CNEDiMTS recommendation without blurring formal appraisal boundaries. If we keep it disciplined, it could be a practical tool rather than an extra layer.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he seems on board. We can now summarize this in language that protects CODIMS: early evaluation of the same device, a few consistent cases, and a retrospective look at what could have been shared in the pre-CNEDiMTS window. I still mean the hospital request-to-rollout phase and broad practical alignment across related variants, but there is no need to unpack that now.
turns.utterance: So, if I try to summarize where we are: we seem aligned on piloting around early evaluation of the same device, in a small number of consistent cases, and then documenting what could have been shared earlier in the pre-CNEDiMTS window. That feels like a manageable first step and also something we could explain clearly to our respective committees.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that summary is usable. The next step should be concrete but still noncommittal: each of us proposes candidate cases and we draft a one-pager. Later we can tighten definitions of the coordination window, dossier structure, and how consistency is shown. For now, I assume she means the same methodological boundaries I do.
turns.utterance: I agree. Why don't we each draft a short list of candidate cases and then a one-page note that sets out the coordination window, the dossier format, and how to show consistency between local and national opinions? That should be enough for a next discussion without locking anyone into a protocol too early.
